diz0: Dislocated Kneecap (Patellar Dislocation): First Aid, Recovery and Exercises | İhsan Eren
diz1: Has your kneecap slipped out of place? What to do straight away, how long to wear a brace, whether it can happen again and when to return to sport. Warning signs and four home exercises.
diz3: Did you feel your kneecap slip out of place during a sudden turn or after a blow to the knee? The kneecap usually moves out of its groove in the thigh bone towards the outside of the knee, and it often pops back by itself. Even if it has gone back, a doctor still needs to examine it. The key to recovery is rebuilding the strength of your thigh and hip muscles.

diz12: A popping feeling in the knee; being unable to straighten the leg.
diz13: Pain, swelling and being unable to put weight on the leg.
diz14: The kneecap may have gone back into place by itself; the swelling and pain still remain.
diz15: A sudden twist with the foot planted, or a direct blow to the knee.
diz16: Weak leg muscles and unusually loose joints raise the risk.
diz17: The shape of the kneecap also plays a part: a small or high-riding kneecap can dislocate more easily.
diz19: Keep your knee still; support it with a rolled-up towel, clothing or cushions while you sit or lie down.
diz20: Do not put weight on the leg or walk on it.
diz21: Do not try to push the kneecap back into place yourself.
diz22: Even if the kneecap has gone back into place, see a doctor as soon as possible; an X-ray is usually needed.
diz25: You can apply ice wrapped in a towel for 10–15 minutes, at least 3 times a day. Keep your leg raised and supported while resting.
diz26: You can take painkillers after checking with your doctor or pharmacist. Less pain makes the exercises easier.
diz27: Do your knee exercises throughout the day to prevent stiffness. Wear the brace for as long as, and within the movement limits, your team advises.
diz29: Avoid twisting and turning movements of the knee. Don’t return to sport until the knee has regained its strength.
diz30: Four exercises to strengthen the knee
diz31: These exercises are for the early stage; if you wear a brace, stay within the limits set by your doctor or physiotherapist. Rest when your thigh muscle tires. As you get stronger, your physiotherapist will move you on to standing exercises such as step-ups.
diz33: Sit or lie with your legs straight and place a rolled-up towel under your knee. Tighten your thigh to press the back of your knee into the towel and lift your heel. Hold for 3 seconds, then lower slowly.
diz34: Lie on your back or sit with your legs straight. Pull your toes towards you, tighten your thigh and, keeping your knee straight, lift your leg about 15 cm. Hold for 3 seconds, then lower slowly.
diz36: Lie on your back or sit. Slide your heel to bend your knee as far as is comfortable, hold briefly, then straighten it. If you wear a brace, do not go past the limit set by your doctor or physiotherapist.
diz38: Lie on your back with your knees bent and feet on the floor; if you wear a brace, bend only as far as allowed. Lift your hips and lower back off the floor, then lower slowly.
diz41: It can. According to a Cochrane review of 10 studies with 519 people, about one in three people treated without surgery after a first dislocation had another dislocation within 2–9 years. After surgery the rate was about one in five; however, the certainty of the evidence is very low, and it is unclear whether surgery clearly improves everyday function.
diz42: Usually not. Surgery may be considered if other structures in the knee are damaged or if the kneecap keeps dislocating. The decision is made with your doctor after examination and imaging.
diz43: How long is a brace worn?
diz44: You may be given a brace after a first dislocation. Your team will decide how long you wear it and how far you can bend your knee. According to one NHS leaflet, a brace may be used for up to two weeks and can be taken off at night, for personal care and for exercises. Some stiffness after the brace comes off is normal.
diz45: When can I return to sport?
diz46: When your knee movement and the strength of your thigh, hamstring and calf muscles match the uninjured side, and you can confidently do what your sport demands, such as running, changing direction and jumping. Sources put this at anywhere from 6–8 weeks to 12–24 weeks. Getting back to everyday activities usually takes 6–12 weeks.
diz47: When you can walk without crutches and do an emergency stop safely.

diz49: When should you go to A&E or see a doctor?
diz50: If your knee has changed shape, you felt a pop, or the knee swelled up quickly
diz51: If bone is visible or there is heavy bleeding
diz52: If you cannot put weight on the leg, or putting weight on it causes sharp pain
diz53: If you have throbbing pain when walking, or swelling, redness or warmth in the calf
diz54: If your knee pain suddenly and severely worsens with a fever
diz55: If you have constant, severe night pain that badly disturbs your sleep
diz56: In the first two cases, go to A&E; if pain stops you moving your leg, call 112. Do not drive yourself. If pain, giving way or difficulty returning to your usual activities continues even after your movement and strength have fully returned, you can also see a specialist.
